sections.subtitle: „Pošalji još“: svjedočanstvo kao misija od Dublina do zatvora
sections.screenshot_description: Goran prepričava molitvu u kuhinji u kojoj je tražio znak je li svjedočenje njegova misija
sections.content:
Goran naglašava da borba ne prestaje: bori se najviše sam sa sobom, zatim sa ženom, djecom i susjedima. **Svaki je dan borba i svaki je dan obraćenje.** U njegovu domu nastoje da molitva ne ostane samo na izgovaranju krunice, nego da prijeđe u djela, u dobrotu prema drugima i pomaganje. Uz ogradu da se ne hvali, jer „to je njegovo, nije moje“, otkriva da su on i supruga razgovorom uputili **više od 60 mladića i djevojaka u zajednicu**. Kad ga nazove netko iz Poljske ili Irske i zahvali mu što mu je spasio sina, odgovara da ga nije spasio on, nego Bog. U tome, kaže, leži radost koju daje život.

Iskreno priznaje i **zasićenost**. Svaki dan tri-četiri puta priča istu priču, a prošle je godine došao do točke kad nije mogao ni jesti ni piti, nego je cijeli dan sjedio ispred kuće i ponavljao isto. Zapao je u krizu, kleknuo u kuhinji i zamolio Isusa da mu pokaže je li svjedočenje njegova misija. Ako nije, neka ljudi malo-pomalo odu, a ako jest, „pošalji još“. To naziva svojom „najvećom greškom“, jer bi sada, kad bi imao snage, mogao imati i deset svjedočanstava dnevno, dok je prije bio zadovoljan s jednim ili dva.

Kaže da još nije posve prihvatio da mu je to misija, ali ide gdje god ga pozovu. Snagu mu daju plodovi: roditelji koji mu dođu na vrata i kažu da im je sin u zajednici već tri godine, ili da je izašao i oženio se.

Voditelj ga na kraju pita gdje je sve svjedočio. Goran nabraja Dublin, gdje je s Vickom govorio pred oko **pet i pol tisuća ljudi 2004. godine**, zatim četiri-pet odlazaka u Ukrajinu te Englesku, Irsku, Italiju i Slovačku, kamo uskoro ponovno putuje.

Najdraža su mu mjesta, kaže, **zatvori i psihijatrijske bolnice**. Publici koja ga sluša njegova je priča možda lijepa, nekoga će učvrstiti u vjeri, a netko će se nasmijati i odmahnuti rukom. Šezdeset bakica od šezdeset do osamdeset godina, šali se uz molbu Bogu za oprost, ne trebaju njegovo svjedočanstvo. Njemu trebaju zatvorenici i pacijenti na psihijatriji, jer ondje zna da mogu nastati plodovi. Susret završava njegovom zahvalom publici „od srca“ i molbom da mu ništa ne zamjere.

magisterium.assessment: Odlomak snažno naglašava obraćenje kao svakodnevni put, molitvu koja se pretvara u dobrotu i služenje te ponizno priznanje da je Bog, a ne svjedok, izvor spasenja; to je skladno s katoličkim razumijevanjem vjere koja djeluje ljubavlju i svjedočanstva riječju i životom. Ipak, tvrdnju da starije žene ne trebaju njegovo svjedočanstvo valja ublažiti: razumljivo je da ga osobito privlači služenje zatvorenicima i bolesnicima, ali potreba za evanđeoskim svjedočanstvom ne može se unaprijed isključiti za neku skupinu ljudi.
concerns: Šaljiva opaska da šezdeset bakica ne treba njegovo svjedočanstvo može zvučati kao da su njihove duhovne potrebe manje ili unaprijed poznate; pastoralno je bolje govoriti o osobitom pozivu služenja zatvorenicima i pacijentima, bez obezvrjeđivanja drugih slušatelja.

Molitveni odgovor „pošalji još” može biti osobno razlučivanje, ali sam po sebi nije dokaz da je svako povećanje broja nastupa Božja volja; odmor, zdravlje i obiteljske obveze također pripadaju odgovornom razlučivanju.
magisterium.enrichment: Crkveno razumijevanje obraćenja ne svodi ga na jednokratan događaj: susret s Kristom poziva na trajnu promjenu života, a vjera treba biti vidljiva u djelima ljubavi i svjedočenju. Služenje zatvorenicima i ljudima u teškim životnim okolnostima ima jasno evanđeosko značenje, no svjedočenje je plod služenja i navještaja, a ne jamstvo da će svaka osoba odmah odgovoriti na isti način.

magisterium.assessment_en: The passage strongly emphasizes conversion as a daily journey, prayer that translates into goodness and service, and humble recognition that God, rather than the witness, is the source of salvation; this is harmonious with the Catholic understanding of faith working through love and witnessing through word and life. Nevertheless, the claim that older women do not need his testimony should be softened: it is understandable that he is particularly drawn to serving prisoners and the sick, but the need for gospel witness cannot be ruled out in advance for any group of people.
magisterium.enrichment_en: The Church's understanding of conversion does not reduce it to a one-time event: the encounter with Christ calls for an ongoing change of life, and faith should be visible in works of love and witnessing. Serving prisoners and people in difficult life circumstances has a clear evangelical meaning, but witnessing is the fruit of service and proclamation, not a guarantee that every person will immediately respond in the same way.
concerns_en: The humorous remark that sixty grandmothers do not need his testimony can sound as though their spiritual needs are less or known in advance; pastorally it is better to speak of a particular calling to serve prisoners and patients, without devaluing other listeners.

The prayerful response “send more” may be personal discernment, but is not in itself proof that every increase in the number of speaking engagements is God's will; rest, health, and family obligations also belong to responsible discernment.

sections.subtitle_en: "Send More": Testimony as a Mission from Dublin to Prisons
sections.screenshot_description_en: Goran recounts the prayer in the kitchen in which he asked for a sign of whether witnessing was his mission
sections.content_en:
Goran emphasizes that the struggle does not stop: he struggles most of all with himself, then with his wife, children, and neighbors. **Every day is a struggle and every day is a conversion.** In his home they strive that prayer does not remain only in reciting the Rosary, but that it passes into deeds, into goodness toward others, and helping. With a caveat that he is not boasting, because "that is His, it is not mine," he reveals that he and his wife through conversation directed **more than 60 young men and women into the community**. When someone calls him from Poland or Ireland and thanks him for saving their son, he answers that he did not save him, but God. In that, he says, lies the joy that life gives.

He also honestly admits **weariness**. Every day three or four times he tells the same story, and last year he reached the point where he could neither eat nor drink, but sat in front of the house all day and repeated the same thing. He fell into a crisis, knelt in the kitchen, and asked Jesus to show him whether witnessing was his mission. If it was not, let people leave little by little, and if it was, "send more." He calls that his "biggest mistake," because now, if he had the strength, he could have as many as ten testimonies a day, whereas before he was satisfied with one or two.

He says that he has not yet completely accepted that this is his mission, but he goes wherever they invite him. Strength is given to him by the fruits: parents who come to his door and tell him that their son has been in the community for three years already, or that he has left and gotten married.

The host asks him at the end where all he has witnessed. Goran lists Dublin, where with Vicka he spoke before about **five and a half thousand people in 2004**, then four or five trips to Ukraine, and England, Ireland, Italy, and Slovakia, where he is soon traveling again.

His favorite places, he says, are **prisons and psychiatric hospitals**. To the audience listening to him, his story is perhaps beautiful, someone will be strengthened in faith, and someone will laugh and wave their hand dismissively. Sixty grandmas from sixty to eighty years old, he jokes while asking God for forgiveness, do not need his testimony. He needs prisoners and patients in psychiatry, because there he knows that fruits can arise. The gathering ends with his thanks to the audience "from the heart" and a plea not to hold anything against him.
